title: Waiting with the Name
hookLine: long waits for news, healing or change
tomorrow: the decision comes, and it's half of what she asked for. now what?

lines: THE ANSWER IS HER OWN NAME.
cards: The school said it would decide by Friday, and it's Tuesday night.
Simran is lying on her bed with the email app open, rereading what she said in the meeting, rewriting it in her head, losing the argument she already finished.
Anyone who has waited for test results, a callback, or a person to wake up knows this loop. The mind keeps chewing because chewing feels like doing something.

teach.b: Simran, the word, means remembering: keeping the Name of the One in mind, often by repeating it. Sikhs repeat Waheguru, sometimes out loud, sometimes on a breath, sometimes moving one bead of a mala for each.
The Japji already knows about the refresh loop.
In its first lines Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase, that thinking it over and over won't get you there, however many times you think it. So simran doesn't fight the waiting mind with more thinking.
It gives the mind something else to hold.

teach.h: A BEAD, A BREATH, A SOUND.
teach.b: Notice how physical it is: a bead under your thumb, a word on your breath, a sound you can hear. That's a detail worth sharing tonight: Sikh remembering is something you can feel in your hands.
Guru Arjan has a line on Ang 819 that people hold onto in long waits.

teach.h: THE HOT WIND DOES NOT TOUCH.
teach.b: In paraphrase: the hot wind does not touch the one who rests in the shelter of the Supreme Lord. The hot wind still blows. Fridays still take forever.

But there's a shelter you can sit in while it blows. Simran sets the phone face down on the carpet. She finds the old mala Bebe gave her, still in her desk drawer, never used, and starts moving it, bead by bead.

how: Sikhs practice simran by repeating the Name, often Waheguru, aloud, under the breath, in kirtan, or with a mala, and some turn to it especially in long waits for news or healing.

games.q: what does “waiting with the name” mean?
o: a promise made to the Guru in exchange for good news
holding the Name in mind, a breath at a time, while you wait
a fast you keep until the news you're hoping for arrives

games.q: waiting, with the senses — tap the pairs.
p: the hot wind does not touch

s: simran means emptying your mind and thinking nothing
it means remembering the Name, often by repeating it: giving the mind something to hold.
Guru Arjan wrote that the hot wind does not touch one who rests in the Lord's shelter
Ang 819, in paraphrase. the wind still blows; there's a shelter to sit in.
the Japji says thinking it through enough times will bring peace
in its first lines Guru Nanak says thinking it over and over won't get you there.

games.q: your cousin is waiting on a college decision and checks the portal every few minutes all night. what fits today best?
o: help her trade the checking for a simple repeated word, a breath at a time.
make a plan to read every review of the school until the email comes.
tell her to stop caring about the result so the waiting stops hurting.
games.why: the Japji says thinking it over won't get you there; simran gives the waiting mind something to hold instead. the result still matters; the loop doesn't help.

practice: Hold a string of beads if you have one; if not, use the joints of your fingers, thumb moving from one to the next. With each breath, move one bead or one joint and say Waheguru silently, or any word that steadies you.
Feel it under your thumb, hear it inside, and let the waiting happen around it.

wordCard.voice: Waiting with the Name. Giving a waiting mind something to hold: the Name, on a breath, a bead at a time.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: simran, remembering the Name, and the friend's own name.

carryVoice: Pocket this: wait with the name, a bead at a time, while the hot wind blows. Tuesday night, day 1726, and the phone is face down.

sources.ref: Ang 1, Japji, first pauri ('sochai soch na hovaee...'), paraphrased
Ang 819, Raag Bilaval, Guru Arjan ('taati vaao na lagaee paarbrahm sharnaaee'), paraphrased
